strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-52xnb41i/call-a2e34467491148c791ff0efbe684a5b5/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a relevant practical question: when task-specific adaptation overtakes zero- or few-shot inference under limited annotation budgets. The break-even framing is intuitive and potentially useful.
The empirical scope is substantial: eight datasets, eight models, four adaptation/inference regimes, many training-set sizes, and additional analyses of model size and quantization.
The extensive repetitions—100 for fine-tuning and 20 for most other settings—are commendable. Explicitly studying sensitivity to seeds is more informative than the common single-run comparison.

The paper provides its prompt and verbalizers, principal hyperparameters, a code link, computational-impact estimates, and unusually candid limitations concerning prompt dependence, possible pretraining contamination, and reduced evaluation sets.
weaknesses: The central variance-adjusted analysis is not statistically valid as presented. Non-overlap between mean minus one standard deviation and mean plus one standard deviation is neither a worst-case guarantee, confidence interval, significance test, nor calibrated low-probability event. It also ignores the covariance induced by shared seeds and splits, unequal repetition counts, and uncertainty in the crossing location. A paired bootstrap or distribution of paired performance differences is needed. This undermines the claimed 100–200% increase in required labels.

The headline claim of “100 labelled samples on average” is not defined and appears inconsistent with Table 1. From that table, the arithmetic mean first break-even points for the best-model comparisons are approximately 680 labels against prompting, 1,941 against in-context learning, and 3,799 against instruction tuning. The aggregation behind Figure 1 is not explained, so the paper’s most prominent quantitative conclusion is presently unsupported.

Several reported results involve oracle-like selection: the best model per approach, the better quantized/full-precision variant for each dataset, and the best in-context shot count observed up to each data size. The manuscript does not establish that these choices were made exclusively on validation data. Selection using test F1 would optimistically bias performance and the resulting break-even points.

The claimed “fair” comparison remains heavily confounded. One prompt optimized around Mistral-7B is used for every model despite the paper itself identifying prompt format as a major source of variation; model families differ in instruction tuning, context length, pretraining, and potential benchmark contamination; and some “specialised small” instruction-tuned models have seven billion parameters and are not smaller than the general models being discussed.

Claims about dataset characteristics are overinterpreted. Four binary and four multiclass datasets cannot isolate effects of class count, input length, task difficulty, domain, imbalance, or pretraining exposure, and no controlled or statistical analysis of these factors is provided. The evidence supports dataset-specific heterogeneity, not the broader conclusion that binary tasks inherently require more labels.

The compute-efficiency analysis is too underspecified to support its recommendations. Approximate FLOPs lack derivations and key assumptions about sequence length, evaluation volume, and deployment horizon; normalizing quantized-model FLOPs by bit width does not directly measure realized computation or latency. Recommendations concerning generation and multilabel tasks also extend beyond the evaluated English classification setting.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: exact checkpoints, LoRA and 4-bit quantization configurations, truncation and preprocessing rules, output parsing, seed lists, early-stopping criteria, and validation-based selection procedures are missing. Repeatedly creating new 60/20/20 splits also mixes evaluation-set sampling variation with training or prompting sensitivity and prevents direct comparison with standard benchmark results. Overall, the study contains valuable experiments, but important reanalysis and targeted reruns are required before it meets the soundness threshold for Findings.

strengths: The paper asks a highly relevant practical question and introduces an intuitive break-even-point framing for comparing task-specialized models with general-purpose LLMs under limited annotation budgets.

The empirical scope is substantial: eight datasets, eight model families, four learning/inference regimes, multiple model sizes, and a quantization analysis. Repeating fine-tuning 100 times and most other experiments 20 times is unusually strong attention to run-to-run variability.

The results expose useful heterogeneity across datasets rather than presenting a single aggregate conclusion. Reporting macro-F1 distributions and both average-based and variance-aware break-even points could support practical model-selection decisions.

The manuscript is generally well organized, provides prompts and major training hyperparameters, releases code, and candidly acknowledges prompt dependence, benchmark contamination, restricted test sets, and unequal evaluation budgets.
weaknesses: The central variance-aware break-even criterion is not statistically justified. Comparing one model's mean minus one standard deviation with another's mean plus one standard deviation is neither a worst-case guarantee nor a confidence interval, and it does not establish the claimed low probability of reversal. It also ignores the covariance induced by matched seeds and uses estimates based on unequal run counts. Consequently, the headline 100–200% increase attributed to variance is meaningful only under an arbitrary heuristic, not as a supported probabilistic conclusion.

Several choices appear to use evaluation performance as an oracle: the paper reports the best model within each approach or size group, selects between quantized and full-precision variants separately by dataset, and reports the best ICL shot count attained up to each available-data size. It is not stated that these choices are made exclusively on validation data. This can produce winner's-curse bias and makes the claimed number of labels needed ill-defined—for example, a point associated with hundreds of available labels may actually use a much smaller, retrospectively selected demonstration set.

The title and abstract's “100 samples on average” claim is not transparently derived. Table 1 contains many break-even points in the hundreds or thousands and several nonexistent second break-even points, but the paper does not specify the aggregation, weighting, treatment of missing points, or uncertainty behind the value 100. Complete numerical results and a preregistered aggregation rule are needed.

The model-size conclusions are strongly confounded by architecture, pretraining, alignment, context length, tuning method, and quantization. Flan-T5, Mistral, Zephyr, LLaMA, and GPT-4o-mini do not form a controlled scaling series, and GPT-4o-mini's parameter count is unknown. Likewise, full tuning of Flan-T5 is compared with quantized LoRA tuning of medium models under reduced training budgets. The evidence therefore supports observations about these checkpoints, not a general conclusion about model size.

The claim that quantization has negligible impact is too broad and is not supported by equivalence tests or a defined negligible-effect threshold; some plotted differences are large. Selecting whichever precision performs best further masks its effect. The compute analysis is also approximate: bit-width-normalized FLOPs are not realized FLOPs, latency, memory, or energy, and the comparison depends on an unspecified deployment workload.

The claimed fairness is weakened by a single prompt optimized around Mistral being reused across model families, different numbers of runs, restricted 1,000-example evaluations for expensive models, reduced instruction-tuning schedules, and model-dependent context limits. Exact checkpoint revisions, LoRA and quantization settings, seed lists, subset grids, output-parsing rules, and validation-selection procedures are also missing from the manuscript.

Claims about binary versus multiclass tasks and tasks requiring “better language understanding” rest on only four datasets per group, with task type, domain, difficulty, class count, and dataset size confounded and no controlled statistical analysis. Possible pretraining contamination of these longstanding benchmarks further limits this interpretation.

These concerns affect the validity of the paper's central quantitative conclusions rather than merely its novelty or prospective impact. A paired statistical analysis, validation-only model/shot selection, transparent aggregation, and narrower causal claims could make the work suitable for Findings, but the present evidence does not yet support a clear positive recommendation.

strengths: Addresses a practically important NLP question: when label-efficient specialization becomes preferable to zero- or few-shot use of general language models. Separating average-performance, variability-aware, and compute considerations is useful.
The empirical coverage is substantial: eight classification datasets, eight models, four adaptation or inference regimes, multiple labeling budgets, and quantized versus non-quantized variants.

The repeated-run effort is a major strength: 100 runs for fine-tuning, 20 for most other approaches, and 10 for GPT-4o-mini. Reporting macro-F1 means and standard deviations explicitly foregrounds randomness that prior comparisons often neglect.

Per-dataset learning curves and break-even tables reveal considerable heterogeneity, including cases where a variance-aware break-even is never reached. This is more informative than reporting only an aggregate result.

The paper is generally clear and candid about its English classification-only scope, single-prompt design, possible pretraining contamination, and reduced large-model evaluation. The public code link and detailed appendices provide a useful basis for replication.
weaknesses: The central “100 labelled samples” headline is not transparently supported. The aggregation behind Figure 1 and “on average 100” is not defined. For fine-tuning, Table 1 reports first break-even points spanning 30–4,250 labels against prompting and 50–9,000 against in-context learning; the corresponding arithmetic means are approximately 680 and 1,941. Averaging performance curves is not equivalent to averaging task-level break-even points and can conceal this heterogeneity. The estimand and aggregation must be specified, and the headline should be scoped accordingly.

The variance-aware criterion is statistically ad hoc. Comparing mean minus one standard deviation for one system against mean plus one standard deviation for another is neither a worst-case bound, a confidence interval, nor a direct estimate of the probability that one system outperforms another. Moreover, changing the test split across repetitions conflates training or exemplar sensitivity with evaluation-sampling variability. Since seeds are aligned, paired performance differences with bootstrap or hierarchical confidence intervals would be more appropriate.

Model and shot selection are insufficiently specified and appear potentially oracle-like. The paper reports the best model or quantization variant per approach and, for in-context learning, the best shot count attained up to each budget, without clearly stating that all such choices are made exclusively using validation data. Selection using displayed test F1 would bias the curves and break-even points.

The claimed fair comparison relies on one prompt engineered for Mistral-7B across every model, even though the paper identifies prompt format as a dominant source of performance variation and recommends model-specific optimization. Consequently, the estimated thresholds characterize this particular prompt and model pool rather than prompting or in-context learning generally.

Several explanatory conclusions exceed what the design identifies. Binary versus multiclass status is confounded with task difficulty, domain, and dataset size; pretraining contamination is invoked despite being unknown; and model-size comparisons mix architectures, context lengths, precision, LoRA versus full tuning, and instruction-tuning histories. These observations should be framed as hypotheses rather than causal findings.

Important reproducibility details remain absent from the manuscript, including complete LoRA and quantization settings, invalid-output handling, exact early-stopping and checkpoint-selection rules, the complete subset grid, and the aggregate break-even computation. The FLOP comparison also combines one-time training and inference without defining a common deployment workload, weakening the compute-efficiency recommendations.

Overall, this is a relevant and promising empirical study, but the unresolved estimand, uncertainty, and selection issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation as written. Reanalysis with paired uncertainty, validation-only selection, a defined aggregation procedure, and prompt-robustness experiments could plausibly make it suitable for Findings in the next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and highly relevant question: when task-specific models become preferable to general-purpose LLMs under limited annotation budgets.

The empirical scope is substantial, covering four adaptation/inference paradigms, eight datasets, several model scales, and quantized variants across learning curves rather than a single few-shot setting.
Using 100 fine-tuning runs and 20 runs for most other conditions is unusually careful. Reusing seeds across models potentially enables informative paired comparisons.

The dataset-level break-even presentation usefully exposes strong heterogeneity that a single aggregate result would conceal. The qualitative finding that modest supervision can make smaller classifiers competitive is supported in several settings.

The authors release code and disclose prompts, broad training settings, computational emissions, and important limitations involving contamination, prompt choice, English-only classification, and reduced evaluation sets.
weaknesses: The central variance-aware criterion is not statistically justified. Non-overlap of mean plus or minus one standard deviation is neither a worst-case guarantee nor a confidence interval and does not establish a stated probability of superiority. The paired runs should instead support confidence intervals or tests on paired performance differences, with uncertainty propagated to each break-even point.

Test sets are resampled with the random seed, so the reported variance conflates training/example-selection sensitivity with evaluation-sample variation. This is especially consequential for deterministic zero-shot prompting, whose variation largely cannot reflect method randomness. The paper therefore cannot cleanly attribute the claimed 100–200% threshold increase to model or approach sensitivity.

Several comparisons appear oracle-selected: in-context learning reports the best result over all shot counts available up to a budget; figures select the best model for each approach; and the main results select whichever precision variant performs best. The manuscript does not state that these choices are made exclusively on validation data. Test-conditioned selection would bias both curves and break-even points.

The headline claim of an average of 100 labels is not traceable to a defined aggregation. In Table 1, the first fine-tuning break-even points average about 680 labels against prompting, 1,941 against in-context learning, and 3,799 against instruction tuning, with several variance-aware comparisons never breaking even. The paper must specify exactly which models, datasets, comparisons, and treatment of missing crossings produce 100.

Claims about model size and dataset characteristics exceed the design. Model size is confounded with architecture, pretraining, alignment, context length, full versus LoRA tuning, and quantization; likewise, binary versus multiclass status is confounded across only eight datasets. These results support descriptive statements about the tested checkpoints, not general conclusions about scaling or causal task characteristics.

The compute-efficiency evidence is inadequate for the recommendations. The FLOP estimates lack a derivation and token/workload assumptions, omit relevant models and API costs, and treat bit-width-normalized 'effective FLOPs' as if it measured actual latency, memory, energy, or monetary cost.

The broad conclusion that 4-bit quantization has negligible impact is based on only two model families, no equivalence testing, and an unspecified quantization configuration. The paper itself reports substantial dataset-specific differences, while choosing the better precision variant in the main comparison further biases results.

Reproducibility is helped by the code link, but the manuscript omits exact checkpoint identifiers, seed lists, subset grids, LoRA configuration, quantizer details, output-parsing rules, and full early-stopping/model-selection procedures. Dense multi-model figures are also difficult to audit numerically.

A single prompt optimized for Mistral is not a controlled comparison across heterogeneous model families, and possible benchmark contamination is particularly serious for these old, widely used datasets. Both limitations directly affect the general-model baselines and hence every headline break-even estimate.

These concerns affect the central numerical claims and require a validation-only selection protocol, statistically principled reanalysis, clearer aggregation, and potentially rerunning experiments with fixed test sets. The empirical effort is promising, but the present evidence is not yet sufficiently sound for Findings.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and highly relevant NLP question: when task-specific fine-tuning or instruction tuning becomes preferable to zero-/few-shot use of general models. The break-even framing is intuitive and potentially useful to practitioners.
The empirical coverage is substantial: four learning paradigms, eight English classification datasets with varied characteristics, and multiple model families and sizes.

Repeating fine-tuning 100 times and most other experiments 20 times (10 for GPT-4o-mini), with matched seeds across models, is considerably more careful than the common single-run evaluation practice.

The authors disclose important limitations, including prompt dependence, possible benchmark contamination, reduced test sets, and proprietary-model costs. They also provide prompts, core hyperparameters, compute estimates, and a public code link.

The manuscript is generally well organized, and its extensive learning curves expose useful dataset-specific heterogeneity rather than reporting only aggregate scores. Assessment is based on the complete manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-3gg8x77m/call-c4ec1db066d84b058bb711b7bac1ef25/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
weaknesses: The central variance-aware analysis is not statistically justified. Requiring mean minus one standard deviation for one model to exceed mean plus one standard deviation for another is neither a worst-case guarantee nor a confidence or significance test. It ignores the paired-seed design, covariance, unequal run counts, multiple comparisons, and uncertainty in the estimated standard deviations. Consequently, the claimed 100–200% increase in required labels does not establish robustness. Paired performance differences with confidence intervals or hierarchical/bootstrap inference are needed.

Several reported results involve post-hoc maximization: the best model per approach or size group, the better quantized/full-precision variant, and, for in-context learning, the best performance among all shot counts up to each budget. The paper does not state that these choices were made exclusively on validation data. If test performance determined them, the break-even points are optimistically biased; even otherwise, the selection protocol and its uncertainty must be specified.

The evaluation mixes sources of variability. Dataset splits and test composition change with the seed, so even deterministic zero-shot prompting has nonzero variation; this is then discussed alongside optimization and example-selection sensitivity as one quantity. Moreover, it is unclear whether methods restricted to 1,000 test examples and fine-tuned models were evaluated on exactly the same paired examples. These sources should be separated and all compared methods evaluated on identical held-out instances.

The headline result that roughly 100 labels suffice is not transparently derived. The paper does not define the averaging method, weighting across datasets/model pairs, treatment of nonexistent break-even points, or interpolation between the sparse label-budget grid. Table 1 itself contains many break-even points in the hundreds or thousands and several NAs. Exact per-comparison values and uncertainty are necessary to support the title-level claim.

Fairness and external validity are limited by using one prompt engineered on Mistral-7B for every model, a mostly small-to-medium set of general models, and benchmarks that may have appeared in instruction-tuning or pretraining data. These factors can readily reverse rankings. The manuscript even infers effects of pretraining inclusion despite acknowledging that inclusion is unknown.

Claims that binary datasets intrinsically require more labels, or that tasks requiring “better language understanding” behave differently, are unsupported causal interpretations of only four heterogeneous datasets per group. Class count is confounded with domain, task difficulty, dataset size, input form, and possible contamination.

The compute and quantization conclusions are also too strong. Approximate FLOPs lack sufficient derivation and omit deployment-volume amortization, while bit-width-normalized FLOPs are not equivalent to measured latency, energy, or hardware cost. Quantization is tested on only two model families without a specified configuration, equivalence margins, or statistical tests, despite some visibly substantial performance gaps.

Important reproducibility details remain absent from the manuscript, including exact checkpoint identifiers, seed and label-budget lists, LoRA and quantization configurations, chat templates, truncation rules, early-stopping/model-selection criteria, and exact shot counts. Dense plots provide few auditable numeric results. The public code link helps, but Findings requires the central analysis to be valid and independently reconstructable; the necessary reanalysis and protocol clarification constitute important revisions suitable for resubmission next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically important NLP question through an intuitive annotation-budget break-even perspective.
The empirical coverage is substantial: eight classification datasets, eight model families, four adaptation regimes, multiple label budgets, and an additional quantization analysis.
Using 100 fine-tuning runs and 20 runs for most other settings demonstrates unusually strong attention to stochastic variation; the shared seeds could support rigorous paired analysis.

The appendices provide prompts, verbalizers, core hyperparameters, per-model curves, compute estimates, and a public code repository. The limitations concerning contamination, prompt choice, and test-set subsampling are candidly acknowledged.
The observed heterogeneity across tasks and models is useful evidence against universal recommendations based on a single benchmark.
weaknesses: The central robustness analysis is not statistically sound as presented. Requiring mean minus one standard deviation for one method to exceed mean plus one standard deviation for another is neither a worst-case guarantee nor a confidence test. It ignores the paired-seed design, conflates test-split variation with training and demonstration-selection randomness, and provides no uncertainty for the estimated crossing point. Consequently, the claimed 100–200% variance-induced increase is tied to an arbitrary threshold rather than a supported probability of superiority.

The headline claim of an average break-even at 100 labels is not auditable: the paper never defines the aggregation across datasets, models, or methods that produces 100. Table 1 instead contains first break-even points ranging from 30 to 20,000 labels and no variance-aware break-even in 7 of 24 comparisons. These censored cases also make a conventional average increase misleading.

The selection protocol is unclear and potentially optimistic. Results use the best-performing model, sometimes the better precision variant, and the best ICL shot count available up to each budget, but do not state that these choices are made exclusively on validation data. The algorithm for converting coarse, noisy learning curves into reported break-even values is also unspecified.

Claims about dataset and model-size effects exceed the evidence. Binary versus multiclass status is confounded with task type, difficulty, dataset source, and possible contamination. Likewise, size is confounded with architecture, pretraining, alignment, context length, and adaptation method; the grouping even labels 7B models medium and an 8B model large. These experiments support descriptive differences among the selected systems, not conclusions that class count or parameter scale caused them.

The comparison characterized as comprehensive and fair uses one prompt optimized for Mistral across all models, while the paper itself recognizes prompt format as highly influential. All datasets are old English benchmarks likely exposed during LLM training, and the specialized baselines omit stronger contemporary encoders and few-shot classification methods. This substantially limits the generality of the practical recommendations.

The compute-efficiency claims are weakly supported: the FLOP estimates omit their calculation assumptions, variable sequence lengths and shot counts, amortization over deployment queries, and several relevant models. Bit-width-normalized 'effective FLOPs' are not a substitute for measured latency, memory, energy, or monetary cost.

Reanalysis with paired performance differences or win probabilities, confidence intervals and censoring-aware break-even estimates, validation-only model and shot selection, and substantially narrower causal claims is needed before the work meets the soundness standard for Findings. These revisions appear feasible for a subsequent cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and practically relevant NLP question: when collecting labels and specializing a model becomes preferable to zero- or few-shot use of a general model.

The experimental sweep is ambitious, covering eight classification datasets, multiple data regimes, four adaptation paradigms, and several model families. The quantization and computational-cost analyses broaden the practical perspective.

Using 100 repetitions for fine-tuning and 20 for most other settings is substantially more careful about randomness than typical single-seed comparisons. Sharing seeds and data subsets across systems could support strong paired analyses.
The manuscript is generally organized clearly, provides prompts and training details in an appendix, acknowledges contamination and prompt sensitivity, and links public code.
weaknesses: The central variance-aware analysis is not statistically valid as presented. Mean minus one standard deviation versus mean plus one standard deviation is neither a worst-case comparison nor a confidence or probability bound. Because systems share seeds, paired performance differences, empirical win probabilities or quantiles, and uncertainty intervals should be analyzed instead. The claimed 100-200% increase in required labels therefore depends on an arbitrary heuristic.

Changing the train/validation/test split with each seed makes the reported standard deviation combine test-set sampling variation, training instability, and in-context-example variation. This prevents the paper from attributing variance to particular learning approaches. A fixed test set and a variance decomposition, or at least paired comparisons on identical test instances, are needed.

Several choices risk oracle evaluation: the manuscript reports the best model within each approach, selects whichever precision variant performs best for each dataset, and takes the best in-context-learning result over all shot counts up to a given budget. It does not establish that these decisions are made solely on validation data. Break-even is also insufficiently defined for noisy, non-monotonic curves that can cross repeatedly.

The headline claim of "100 labelled samples on average" is not accompanied by a precise aggregation formula and is difficult to reconcile with Table 1, which contains many break-even points in the hundreds or thousands and several unavailable second break-even points. Claims that binary tasks, input length, or required language understanding explain the differences are inferred from only eight heavily confounded datasets without controlled or statistical analysis.

The comparison does not cleanly isolate specialization or model size. The same prompt, optimized for Mistral-7B, is used for every model despite prompt sensitivity being identified as the strongest factor; tuning regimes mix full fine-tuning, LoRA, and quantization; and fixed hyperparameters are not shown to be competitive. Moreover, the "specialized small versus general large" grouping includes task-tuned 7B models and relatively small general models, so architecture, pretraining, alignment, size, and adaptation are conflated.

The compute-efficiency evidence is too weak for the practical recommendations: FLOPs are only approximate, assumptions and workload amortization are underexplained, and bit-width-normalized FLOPs do not establish realized latency, memory, energy, or cost. The broad quantization conclusion is based on only two 7B families in prompting/ICL, lacks equivalence tests, and conflicts with visibly substantial losses in some reported settings.

Reproduction details remain incomplete, including exact checkpoint revisions, LoRA and quantization configurations, chat templates, output parsing and invalid-generation handling, seed lists, and software versions. Dense plots replace many exact numerical results, while the hosted GPT endpoint is not deterministic or stable over time. The large compute requirement further increases the importance of releasing per-run predictions and measurements.

The experimental effort is valuable, but these issues affect the validity of the paper's defining break-even and variance claims rather than merely its novelty or presentation. A publishable revision appears feasible next cycle through leakage-free selection, paired statistical reanalysis, transparent aggregation, and substantially narrower claims, but the current evidence does not yet meet the soundness bar for Findings.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a practical, highly relevant NLP question and compares four adaptation paradigms across eight models and eight classification datasets. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-8yrabxx7/call-89075bcb9b894f2f9adfd91945073ab6/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The extensive repetition—100 runs for fine-tuning and generally 20 for other approaches—and reporting of means and standard deviations are valuable. Few comparative studies examine randomness at this scale.

The per-dataset learning curves and break-even table reveal substantial heterogeneity that a single full-data comparison would obscure. Including instruction tuning, quantization, and approximate computation costs broadens the empirical scope.

The paper provides code, prompts, verbalizers, principal hyperparameters, and model versions, and candidly acknowledges limitations involving prompt choice, test-set subsampling, English-only benchmarks, and possible pretraining contamination.
weaknesses: The central “average+variance” breakpoint is not statistically valid as interpreted. Requiring mean minus one standard deviation to exceed the competing mean plus one standard deviation is neither a worst-case guarantee, a confidence interval, nor evidence of a low error probability. It ignores the paired-seed design, covariance, unequal run counts, uncertainty in estimated moments, and multiple comparisons. Consequently, the claimed 100–200% variance-induced increase in label requirements is not adequately supported.

The model-selection protocol appears oracle-like. Results use the best model per approach, the better quantized or full-precision version per dataset, and the best in-context shot count observed up to each budget, without specifying that these choices were made exclusively on validation data. Selecting them from test performance would bias all reported breakpoints. Training curves may also stop once fine-tuning wins, so a first crossing is not shown to remain a crossing.

The headline “100 labelled samples on average” is not defined or reconciled with the principal numerical table. The first breakpoints in Table 1 average approximately 680 labels against prompting, 1,941 against in-context learning, and 3,799 against instruction tuning. An explicit population of comparisons, aggregation rule, treatment of missing breakpoints, and uncertainty estimate are essential.

Variance across runs mixes training randomness with newly sampled 60/20/20 data splits and hence test-set composition. Moreover, expensive large-model conditions use only 1,000 test examples and fewer repetitions, while the paper does not establish an identical evaluation sample for every compared model. Raw standard deviations therefore do not isolate model sensitivity and may not be comparable.

The claimed size analysis is heavily confounded by architecture, pretraining, alignment, context length, tuning method, and precision. The “specialized” pool includes 7B models, the “general” pool includes small Flan-T5, and GPT-4o-mini has an undisclosed size. These experiments support observations about particular checkpoints, not the causal conclusion that model size does not help.

A single prompt engineered on Mistral-7B is used for heterogeneous chat, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder models, even though the paper itself says prompt format is a major performance determinant. Likewise, one largely fixed fine-tuning recipe is used across datasets and data regimes. Without validation-based, model-appropriate prompt and hyperparameter robustness checks, the comparison is not convincingly fair.

Claims about dataset characteristics are underidentified: four binary language-understanding datasets are contrasted with four generally easier topic/intent datasets, so class count is confounded with task, length, domain, separability, and contamination. The paper admits that pretraining inclusion is unknown but nevertheless invokes it as an explanation. Recommendations concerning generation, multilingual, and multilabel tasks extend beyond the experiments.

The compute-efficiency evidence is too coarse for the conclusions. Fixed approximate FLOP totals omit a transparent derivation, token lengths, number of in-context examples, deployment query volume, latency, memory, and API cost; normalizing FLOPs directly by bit width is not a demonstrated hardware cost measure. The broad quantization recommendation is based on only two 7B models and one quantization level, despite sizable differences on several datasets and no significance analysis.

Reporting issues further reduce confidence: Table 1 labels a change from 100 to 500 as a 500% increase rather than 400%, treatment of nonexistent second breakpoints in averages is unspecified, full numerical results are absent, and the largest figures are too crowded to audit. Exact seeds, checkpoint identifiers, LoRA and quantization configurations, output parsing, and selection procedures are also insufficiently documented in the manuscript.

These concerns affect both primary research questions rather than presentation alone. A credible revision would require a prespecified validation-selection protocol, paired statistical inference with breakpoint uncertainty, consistent held-out evaluation, reconciliation of the headline statistic, and narrower causal claims; this is substantial but plausibly achievable for a next-cycle resubmission.

strengths: The manuscript addresses a concrete and practically relevant NLP question: when supervised specialization becomes preferable to zero-/few-shot use of general language models. The break-even framing is intuitive and potentially useful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/emnlp2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-dmb412pa/call-29708a71fc064cc4ab82c126ab4c697b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical coverage is substantial: eight English classification datasets, eight model families, four learning regimes, multiple label budgets, and 100 fine-tuning or 20 other runs (10 for GPT-4o-mini). Reporting run-to-run dispersion and using common seeds across models are valuable choices.

The paper is generally well organized, publishes code, specifies the common prompt and several core hyperparameters, and candidly acknowledges prompt dependence, possible benchmark contamination, restricted task/language coverage, evaluation subsampling, and computational cost.
The results provide useful descriptive evidence that conclusions vary greatly across datasets and models, and that small supervised encoders remain competitive for classification.
weaknesses: The headline result—“100 labelled samples on average”—is neither formally defined nor reconciled with the main results. From Table 1, the first break-even points for the best models average approximately 680 labels against prompting, 1,941 against in-context learning, and 3,799 against instruction-tuning; even the corresponding medians exceed 100 for two of the three comparisons. The paper must specify the model pairs, weighting, treatment of missing break-even points, and averaging method behind 100, and report uncertainty over each discretely located breakpoint.

The central variance analysis lacks a statistically valid interpretation. Defining a second breakpoint by mean minus one standard deviation exceeding the competitor's mean plus one standard deviation does not provide a worst-case bound, confidence interval, hypothesis test, or calibrated probability that one method wins. Because seeds are shared, paired score differences should be analyzed directly; marginal standard-deviation bands discard their covariance. Moreover, changing the test split across runs mixes evaluation-sample variation with training and in-context-example sensitivity. Consequently, claims about low failure probability and a 100–200% variance-induced increase are not adequately established.

Several reported curves appear to involve post-hoc oracle selection: the best model is chosen for each approach, quantized or full-precision results are selected per dataset, and ICL reports the best shot count attained anywhere up to each budget. The manuscript does not state that these decisions are made exclusively on validation data or account for their selection uncertainty. If evaluation scores were used, this is test leakage; even otherwise, the resulting upper envelopes do not represent a fixed, deployable procedure and can shift the break-even points.

The “small specialized versus large general” construct is not consistently instantiated: specialized systems include 7B Mistral/Zephyr models, while general systems include the much smaller Flan-T5-base. Likewise, the model-size conclusion compares unrelated architectures, pretraining corpora, alignment procedures, context lengths, and prompt compatibility rather than controlled within-family scales. Claims attributing effects to class count or task difficulty are also confounded because the four multiclass datasets are comparatively easy topic/intent datasets, while the binary set contains substantially different tasks. These findings should be framed as associations within the tested configurations.

The single Mistral-oriented prompt materially weakens cross-model comparisons, especially given the paper's own conclusion that prompt format is highly influential. There is no prompt-robustness analysis, invalid-output rate, or sufficiently detailed output-parsing description. Possible pretraining contamination of these old benchmarks further prevents clean data-efficiency comparisons.

The quantization and compute conclusions are overgeneralized. Quantization is tested on only two model families, with sizeable reported differences for some Zephyr/dataset combinations, yet the recommendation is stated broadly. The FLOP table lacks derivations, token counts, shot counts, deployment-query assumptions, and a clear justification for its bit-width-normalized “effective FLOPs”; it also does not establish the claimed compute comparability across all evaluated models.

Reproduction from the manuscript remains difficult despite the code link: exact checkpoint identifiers, dataset revisions, seed and nested-subsampling protocol, LoRA and 4-bit configurations, sequence truncation and chat templates, validation/model-selection procedure, and machine-readable per-run results are not reported. The most complete result figure is too crowded to recover exact comparisons, while reproducing the study reportedly requires roughly 4,000 GPU-hours plus a proprietary API.

These concerns affect the validity of the central numerical and variance-aware claims, rather than merely novelty or presentation. A next-cycle revision could plausibly succeed by reanalyzing paired runs with prespecified validation-only selection, documenting the 100-label aggregation, releasing numerical results, and narrowing or properly controlling the size, dataset-characteristic, quantization, and compute claims; the current version does not yet meet the soundness threshold for Findings.

Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess the validity of the central claims, the suitability and rigor of the methodology, the adequacy of supporting evidence, reproducibility, clarity, and relevance to computational linguistics and natural language processing. Evaluate the contribution in light of its stated aims. Distinguish evidence of soundness from subjective interest, novelty, and prospective impact.

Findings requires adequate soundness and reproducibility. Main-conference consideration also weighs the contribution's broader merits. A sound Findings recommendation need not imply that the paper has a technical defect. Do not compute the overall assessment by averaging separate dimensions or treating personal excitement as a substitute for evidence. Explain the decisive strengths and weaknesses.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, or 5.

Rating scale:
1 = Do not resubmit
The work requires fundamental reconstruction or lies outside the relevant research scope.

1.5 = Resubmit after next cycle
Substantial work is required, on a timescale longer than the next review cycle.

2 = Resubmit next cycle
Important revisions remain, but a revised submission could reasonably be ready for the next cycle.

2.5 = Borderline Findings
The case for Findings is close, with unresolved concerns preventing a clear positive recommendation.

3 = Findings
The paper supports a sound and reproducible contribution suitable for Findings.

3.5 = Borderline Conference
The main-conference recommendation is close; explain what limits confidence in that recommendation.

4 = Conference
The paper warrants main-conference publication based on its supported contribution and overall merits.

4.5 = Borderline Award
The paper is a plausible outstanding-paper candidate, with reservations about that distinction.

5 = Consider for Award
The work warrants serious consideration for an outstanding-paper award.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

The empirical scope is substantial: four learning paradigms, eight models, eight classification datasets, numerous label budgets, and an additional quantization comparison.

Using 100 fine-tuning runs, 20 runs for most other approaches, and shared seeds demonstrates unusually serious attention to randomness. These data could support a rigorous paired uncertainty analysis.

The paper reports heterogeneous and negative results, including nonexistent break-even points, and provides prompts, verbalizers, core hyperparameters, a public code link, limitations, and a compute-impact statement.
weaknesses: The central variance-aware break-even criterion is not statistically valid as presented. Non-overlap of mean plus or minus one standard deviation is neither a worst-case bound nor a confidence interval and does not establish a calibrated low probability of performance reversal. It also ignores paired covariance despite shared seeds, uncertainty from unequal run counts, and multiplicity across budgets and model choices. The claimed 100–200% and up-to-3000% increases therefore require reanalysis using paired per-seed differences, bootstrap intervals, or explicit probability thresholds.

Several choices appear to use reported performance as an oracle: the best model within each approach or size, the best quantized/full-precision variant for each dataset, and the best ICL shot count attained up to each budget. No validation-only or nested selection protocol is specified. Consequently, the curves may combine different systems and test-selected configurations, biasing the break-even estimates.

The headline “100 labelled samples on average” is not transparently defined or supported by a corresponding table. For example, simple means of the first fine-tuning break-even points in Table 1 are approximately 680 versus prompting, 2066 versus ICL, and 3799 versus instruction tuning, with individual values reaching 4250, 9000, and 20000. Moreover, the apparent best-specialized aggregation includes 7B instruction-tuned models, which are not small relative to several general-model comparators.

Claims about binary tasks, language-understanding difficulty, model size, and pretraining exposure are insufficiently identified. Only eight datasets are used, and class count is confounded with domain, task difficulty, input length, and possible contamination. A single prompt engineered for Mistral-7B is reused across architectures, which can materially distort model-size rankings.

The compute and quantization conclusions are overextended. The FLOP table omits formulas and assumptions about sequence length, label budget, number of shots, evaluation volume, and deployment amortization; its stated compute comparability holds only up to two-shot ICL although experiments select many more examples. Quantization is tested on only Mistral and Zephyr, has notable dataset-specific exceptions, and is not statistically tested, so recommending it broadly—including for instruction tuning—is unsupported.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the code link: exact checkpoint revisions, LoRA configuration, quantization settings, chat templates, invalid-output handling, subset grid, seed list, and selection algorithm are not specified. Together with unresolved benchmark contamination and proprietary GPT-4o-mini evaluation, these central issues require substantial reanalysis and clarification before the work is sound enough for Findings.
